This study introduces a novel time-series model called TV-PARX, which is based on a time-varying Poisson process and is designed to account for the nonlinear dynamics and potential structural breaks often observed in real-world data. Due to the nature of count data, linear models such as the standard PARX model have limited predictive capability. Conversely, sudden changes in events can cause significant deviations from the assumptions of the Poprocess, rendering it ineffective. By incorporating a moving average of exogenous covariates to determine the parameters of the Poprocess at any given time step, the TV-PARX model achieves a flexible framework suitable for various applications. We present theoretical and empirical evidence demonstrating the TV-PARX model's capacity to capture the nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks exhibited by the Moon Dust and Twitter Fire datasets. Additionally, we develop a novel estimation procedure based on the minimum contrast method and a theoretical framework based on probability metrics to analyze the asymptotic properties of the estimated parameters.

In 10/2019, an interesting study was conducted which demonstrates the ability to measure the vertical aerosol optical depth over a broad field of view without the need for initial absolute calibration. This research, published in Journal of Quantitative Spectroscopy and Radiative Transfer, reveals that wide-field photometry can effectively contribute to aerosol optical depth measurements across large areas. The ElTeTe experiment, which served as the foundation for this research, involved a field test in the Canary Islands that aimed to develop an unrestrained measurement system for aerosol optics that spans a broad area. During the course of the experiment, a campaign was carried out in the island of Tenerife that aimed to experiment with the ElTeTe setup and collect data on aerosols that spans a large area. The researchers found that wide-field photometry can accurately determine aerosol optics levels that span a broad area, even without the need for initial absolute calibration. In addition to the ElTeTe experiment, a complementary experiment was organized that aimed to experiment with the relationship between fields aerosols that spans a large area and those measured by a radiometer that is precisely calibrated. The researchers found that wide-field photometry can accurately reflect aerosol optics levels that spans a large area, with a minor discrepancy observed between the two measurement methods. Building on the results obtained from the ElTeTe experiment, a method was developed that allows for the determination of broad-area aerosol optics levels without the need for initial absolute phot

This study compares three molecular dynamics simulation methods—Langevin dynamics and two Hamiltonian approaches, Split-Operator and Leap-Frog, when exploring the conformational space of an amino acid fragment known as alanine dipeptide. To facilitate this analysis, we developed an open-source Python library called BioSimJAX that integrates classical molecular simulations with Bayesian statistical methods for computing potential energy surfaces using ensemble-based Gaussian processes. In our findings, we observe that while Langevin dynamics may slow down the simulation process, it effectively reduces numerical oscillations. Furthermore, we determine that the Split-Operator method offers an more accurate potential energy surface approximation compared to the Leap-Frog method, but at the cost of slightly higher computational time. All results in this study support the use of fourth-order Runge-Kutta time stepping method with an 0.001 femtosecond time step in ensemble-based Gaussian process simulations.

Variational methods in quantum field theory present an optimization challenge that can be addressed by applying the Euler-Arnold equations. This work aims to adapt the Euler-Arnold framework to specific quantum field theory models, including scalar and spinor field oscillators, as well as their non-linear variants, and to derive variational Hamiltonians for these models. Furthermore, we extend these models by incorporating an external source and deriving the corresponding Nonlinear Schrödinger and Dirac equations in an optimized form. A comparison with standard approaches demonstrates the advantages of using the Euler-Arnold framework.

The interaction between heavy quarks is extensively studied, using the color Emission Approximation (CEA) to analyze their production and decay processes. This note focuses on the relationship between a charm and an anti-charm quark that share the same mass and spin but differ in charge, and the particles that result from their interaction. Similar to previous studies on heavy quark interactions initiated by two quarks of the same charge, this work examines the particles produced when a charm quark and an anti-charm quark are in a state with S=0 and 0^+ within the first few energy levels.

This work delves into the optimization problems of fair and total throughput in a broad spectrum signal formation context. Due to the discrete and continuous nature of sub-space allocations, we employ a multi-variable integer programming approach. By leveraging an ordering system for eigenvectors, we develop an efficient algorithm to maximize fair and total throughput. Our findings show that fair throughput is determined by an integer value and can be computed through an efficient search of possible values, resulting in a polynomial time solution for fair throughput optimization. Furthermore, we derive the precise complexity for determining feasible point existence and polynomial time conditions for fair-throughput optimization.

This study compares various regularization methods used in operator formalism to control divergences and examines their impact on the obtained functions in a study of quantum field theory. Additionally, we investigate the purpose of dglap evolution when fitting pdfs at distinct scales and discover that certain methods can substitute for this process. A new and innovative method is proposed, evaluated, and incorporated into a public online tool for exploring quantum field theory experiments.

This study investigates a nonlinear reacting flow model in a 2D vertical channel, driven by a heat source and fuel source, and subject to a strong reverse flow at the channel's inlet. Utilizing a spectral method, the model is solved within a linearized framework, and various combustion models are evaluated to determine their compatibility with the linearized framework, particularly in handling turbulent fluctuations of temperature and species concentration. The Euler-Lagrange approach is employed to model droplet dynamics, while both the Flame Surface Density (FSD) and Thickened Flame (TF) methods are used to simulate flame dynamics. After assessing the suitability of each model for use in a linearized framework, the TF method is selected and a DNS is conducted to perform a high-resolution simulation of a compressible turbulent droplet-laden flame, driven by the Kelvin-Helmholtz and Rayleigh-Tami instability modes. The results of the DNS are analyzed to produce detailed 3D visualizations of the flow, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Euler-Lagrange approach in capturing the dynamics of a highly turbulent, compressible flame surrounding a breaking vortex and the accuracy of the TF model in predicting reacted gas distribution.

This paper proposes a nonlocal theory of gravity that can be directly
linked to observable quantities, defying the conventional nonlocal models
that rely on intricate definitions unlikely to have any physical significance.
Our suggestion indicates that at large scales, general relativity is an
approximation that results from ignoring the nonlocal influence of dark
energy that can be expressed as an effective tension within the universe.
This explanation naturally accounts for the universe's accelerated
expansion and predicts its value with perfect accuracy.

A notable phenomenon observed in high multiplicity proton-proton (pp) collisions is the possible creation of more complex particles with non-zero non-eternal quantum numbers, such as (K+, K-). A comprehensive (E)pp particle and particle type formation model is proposed to explain the transition from proton-proton collisions to collisions between nuclei, focusing on the relationship between the number of participating gluons and the possible overabundance of exotic particles. The (E)pp model predicts the overabundance of exotic particles in collisions between nuclei and compares predictions to experimental (PbPb) and (AuAu) data, showing strong agreement with overabundance measurements of exotic particles and angular, transverse, and total energy distributions of particles. The overabundance of exotic particles is found to be inextricably linked to the total energy of produced particles, as opposed to the number of binary collisions, and the (E)pp model provides an accurate account of the angular and transverse distribution of hadrons in collisions between nuclei, aligning with experimental data.

Now, we are analyzing a sub-component of the neutron star community called the NS LMXB segment, which includes systems like A0620-00, GS2023, and A0535-26. By investigating this sub-community, we aim to comprehend the formation processes that give rise to radio loud and quiet millisecond radio pulsars within the Galaxy. A neutron star LMXB system is defined as a NS merging with a companion star in a system that emits little to no X-rays and shows no optical variability, except for tidal disruption events. Our analysis reveals that the NS LMXB system population is estimated to be between 20 and 200, based on depletion analyses of the NS population and considering varying timescales of re-ignition and TDE events. We also explore the characteristics of these systems, including their distribution across the Galaxy, formation rates, and masses, finding that they are primarily located in the disc, formed at rates similar to the millisecond radio pulsar population, and have average masses within the range of 1.4 to 1.6 solar masses. Additionally, we explore the significance of disk or bulge formation rates and the importance of recycling and TDE events, concluding that this sub-community plays a minor role in the overall neutron star community but is vital in understanding the birth processes of radio pulsars within the Galaxy. Bipartite graphs that can be represented by intervals on a line are known to have a bipartite interval depth not exceeding one. Although drawing these graphs in a planar manner is straightforward, bipartite graphs with a depth of two present more challenges. We demonstrate that for any such graph G, a bipartite drawing with a depth of one can be achieved by modifying at most two points on the interval representation. Consequently, such a drawing becomes possible by creating a limited number of additional vertices, thus resulting in a bipartite drawing that is essentially one-point.

Degrading a CPU's performance intentionally has been used to make certain attacks, such as Flush+Reload, more effective more easily.  While previous methods of degrading a CPU's performance more efficiently more strongly relied on cache pollution as a mechanism, this paper introduces a different approach that relies on increasing the cache line residence time by reducing CPU clock speed in real time.  The proposed method, called HyperDegrade, is the first to focus on slowing down a CPU's clock in real time to make cache-based attacks more effective more easily.  As it does not require any specific data format to slow down the CPU's clock in real time, HyperDegrade proves difficult to resist in practical scenarios.  As HyperDegrade's proposed method of delivering instructions to slow down the CPU's clock in real time builds on existing degradation techniques, it enhances their efficacy more easily more easily with minimal overheads and with little modification required.  As HyperDegrade is demonstrated to reduce the number of required traces by two orders of magnitude in two well-known Cache Timing Attacks (CTA), it proves its efficacy more easily more easily and stands out as the first to focus on slowing down a CPU's clock in real time to make Cache Timing Attacks more effective easily with little overhead.

A new variant of the traditional 2-brick model is introduced in this paper, termed the "diagonal-brick model." Within this updated framework, it is demonstrated that knot and link configurations can be replicated using bricks that move only diagonally, even when bricking lines that move similarly and are subject to the conventional Reidemeister III move. By combining previous findings, it is established that all possible knot and link models can be achieved using a model where bricks are moved solely diagonally and are also allowed to perform the diagonal-brick version of the overcrossing move.

The challenges faced by agents within a shared environment play a pivotal role in shaping the behavior of multi-agent systems.  We examine a scenario where an overarching controller makes decisions on which tasks difficult and diverse to resolve should be presented to learning agents for potential resolution.  Resolved and unresolved tasks, respectively, contribute to the financial gains and losses experienced by the collective system.  Optimal policies in such environments tend to reserve resources for future, potentially easier tasks while disregarding probability assignments for simpler tasks that could be readily resolved.  The ideal strategy evolves over time, adapts to the characteristics of upcoming tasks, and is influenced by the initial resources available to the system.  Obtaining insights into the optimal policy that maximizes long-term gains is possible through a closed-form solution, and we further explore the impact of task difficulty distributions, time horizons, and initial resource allocations on optimal behavior through simulations.  Our findings reveal that obtaining insights on optimal decision-making are profoundly impacted by the characteristics of tasks and system parameters.

A simultaneous action of a collection of groups on a set is regular when no non-trivial combination of the groups leaves any set point unchanged. We examine the connection between regular actions and Cartesian decompositions, with examples including classic cases like Latin squares from regular actions of single groups, and more complex multi-networks from regular actions of multiple groups. We also explore the role of diagonal groups within regular actions, demonstrating their exclusion from certain regular simultaneous actions of two groups, D and E, when specific conditions are not satisfied, which are not dominant in their action on a given set. We further prove that if the decimal representations of the sizes of the two sets are prime numbers with distinct factors, the diagonal groups D^e and E^e corresponding to action components are not regular for these components, necessitating a revised term ultra-dominant.

A novel design for a sagnac interferometer has been developed that incorporates a sloshing pattern to achieve an enhanced sensitivity to linear accelerations, making it comparable to that of linear interferometers. This sloshing-Sagnac design also retains the immunity to laser intensity fluctuations that typical recirculating linear interferometers suffer from. A theoretical analysis indicates that by optimizing the sloshing-Sagnometer sloshing-Sagnac interferometer's parameters, its sensitivity to phase shifts caused by linear accelerations can be made equivalent to that of a 4-kilometer-long linear interferometer's sensitivity to quantum shot noise limitations, despite having only 40-centimeter-end mirrors. A prototype sloshing-Sagnac device has been constructed and deployed in a laboratory setting to verify the characteristics of this new design.

To enhance random access efficiency in systems with extremely large MIMO (NOVR-XL), an innovative protocol is proposed for XL-MIMO networks. The NOVR-XL protocol simplifies the random access process by eliminating the report of reserved subchannels and dividing the transmission of selected data into multiple, independent segments that can be accessed simultaneously. In an NOVR-XL system, various segments of different data sets can successfully reconstruct and be decoded, even in the event of failures or successes among the segments. Simulations show that the NOVR-XL protocol significantly boosts random access efficiency in systems with a high likelihood of data transmission requests and a low probability of segment decoding success. The benefits become even more pronounced as the size of the data set grows or when the probability of segment decoding success decreases.

Recent experiments show that integrating N-gram models with neural language models can benefit various language-related tasks, including machine translation, source language summarization, and topic modeling. However, the significant computational cost of N-gram models limits their use in combining with neural models. This paper proposes a fast approximation of conditional N-gram models based on sample reduction and then tests the improved model in sequence labeling and combining with neural models in machine translation and summarization tasks. The results demonstrate that the improved model can closely mimic the original conditional N-gram model while significantly reducing memory usage with little loss in performance.

Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems processing scanned ballots face issues with errors and out-of-vote situations due to handwriting variability. To resolve these problems in Ecuador's vote tabulation system, a spell-correcting component was integrated before the OCR pipeline, utilizing cluster-based unsupervised learning. This approach reduced errors and enhanced the accuracy of vote counting, demonstrating its effectiveness through real-world vote data. The solution's efficiency and low data requirements make it suitable for use in similar systems operating with handwritten votes.

This study investigates the circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere modified with initial conditions resembling those of a Martian storm, revealing remarkable similarities to baroclinic storms observed on Mars without any direct programming of such storm-like behaviors.

Special functions such as the Gamma function can be effectively represented through contour integrals in the complex plane. A Hankel path within the complex plane is essential for calculating these integrals. A new, highly efficient algorithm is proposed that can compute any arbitrary positive real number using the Gamma function through contour integral representation, as well as any negative real number via reflection formula. Furthermore, the Gamma function can be directly calculated for complex numbers with a positive real part through the contour integral representation. This efficient representation leads to the precise computation of functions such as the Riemann zeta function and its derivatives, as well as the $k$-folded zeta function, by utilizing Hankel path sampling for their complex number inputs. The implementation of the contour-integral based algorithm and its derivatives are efficiently executed through the use of the trapezoidal rule with parameter shifting, as well as the fast Fourier transform for contour discretization, demonstrating its superiority over traditional real-axis sampling methods in handling these functions.

This research presents a novel stochastic hydrodynamic scheme to handle quantum systems far from equilibrium, specifically designed to capture collective effects without complex hydrodynamic simulations. The method builds on existing quantum optics approaches by incorporating collective reactions through a simple linearized hydrodynamic step between light scattering and emission processes, allowing for an accurate reproduction of quantum fluid behavior within a basic hydrodynamic model. The scheme's validity is verified through tests on Roton Quantum Correlations and BEC Quantum Correlations, demonstrating its effectiveness in simulating complex quantum fluids without full hydrodynamic simulations, even under highly non-equilibrium conditions.

Teacher-Student architectures are widely used to train lightweight student networks by guiding them with the predictions of a more capacity-intensive teacher network.  Traditional Teacher-Student models rely on direct student-teacher connections, which result in a substantial growth in parameters and computational operations for the teacher network.  To address this issue, we propose a Teacher-Student architecture that is indirect, integrating a highly optimized intermediate network between the teacher and student.  Our suggested teaching methods include utilizing both raw inputs and teacher predictions to train the intermediate network, as well as a method to train the intermediate network to emulate the teacher network's capabilities.  Evaluating our proposed Teacher-Student architecture on the ImageNet10 and Cropset20 datasets reveals that students taught with this design outperform students taught through direct teacher-student connections.  Specifically, the best-performing student networks exhibit impressive achievements that exceed the teacher network's performance, demonstrating that teacher capabilities need not limit student potential.

The problem of inferring the most probable assignment in graphical models, or equivalently, to optimize a function that has a structured format, is known to be computationally intensive. We present an advanced version of the Bucket Elimination algorithm that can be used to precisely solve this problem, and also to approximately solve it when necessary, with little computational effort. Our enhanced method modifies the basic Bucket Elimination to keep track of what has been computed, resulting in an approximately solved problem in cases where an exact solution is beyond reach within a reasonable amount of time. The enhanced Algorithm can immediately precisely solve the problem in cases where it is tractable, with little additional work, then use an approximation strategy in cases that are intractable, resulting in an approximately solved problem in most cases, and also to precisely solve the problem in cases that are fully tractable with little additional work. We propose an enhanced version of Bucket Elimination that can be used to precisely solve the maximum marginal inference problem in graphical models, and also to approximately solve it in most cases in which an exact solution is beyond computational reach within a reasonable amount of time, allowing for exact solutions to be achieved in cases that are tractable with little additional work.

A formula for the centralizer $Z(n)(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is given in terms of the centralizers $Z(d)(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ whose corresponding degree $d$ is a divisor of $n$. Furthermore, we provide an expression for the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the centralizer $Z(n)(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. Given the factorization properties of integers into prime numbers, we can decompose the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the centralizer $Z(n)(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ into its constituent parts corresponding to prime degrees. A detailed examination of the Hilbert-Poincaré series for centralizers $z(p)(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ for all prime degrees $p \le 19$ is carried out. Based on the obtained results, we propose formulas for the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the centralizers $z(p)(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ for prime degrees $p=17$ and $p=19$.

Statistical significance assessments can be performed using paired-permutation tests via an established exact algorithm or an efficient Monte Carlo approximation method. While the exact algorithm guarantees precision, its computational demands are high, particularly for larger datasets. In contrast, the Monte Carlo approximation offers a more efficient alternative with minimal computational costs but sacrifices some level of accuracy. Although the decisive paired-permutation test and the corresponding Lempel-Ziv data compression tests appear to compete efficiently for small datasets, the exact algorithm's high computational complexity makes it difficult to surpass the Monte Carlo approximation for larger datasets. However, an improved version of the Lempel-Ziv tests has been achieved through an innovative set of modifications, resulting in an exact algorithm that is more precise than previously accomplished versions. The enhanced Lempel-Ziv tests' computational complexity is now comparable to the best exact algorithms for small alphabets, and for a dataset of 10000 elements with a binary configuration, the improved exact paired-permutation test matches the Monte Carlo approximation with a significance level of 0.0001 with just a single pass over the data, requiring negligible computational time.

While individual hadron species are being measured across a wide range of collision energies and geometries, a striking observation emerges when looking at the transverse momentum dependence of the elliptic and triangular flow coefficients, $v_n/p_T$, for different particle types. This pattern, consistent over a broad spectrum of collision energies from 10 to 200 GeV, warrants a theoretical explanation that goes beyond a local quark-gluon medium temperature and pressure description.

This study addresses a scenario where a sensor, with a restricted field of view, actively searches for targets within a given area, and acknowledges that targets have movement patterns that are initially unknown but confined to a specific range. The objective is to minimize the probability that undetected targets go unnoticed. A dynamic programming approach is proposed to compute the optimal search strategy in a discrete-time system and is shown to have a computational complexity that is significantly lower than previously calculated methods for calculating optimal controls. Furthermore, simulations are conducted to illustrate that using intervals to represent the probability range of undetected targets' locations can lead to a more efficient computation of the optimal control compared to a system where precise locations are known. By leveraging the principles of interval arithmetic, the method can determine the optimal control with a reduced computational complexity, and a recursive algorithm is developed to compute the optimal control in a discrete-time system and is shown to have a computational complexity that is lower than previously calculated methods.

Football games are increasingly computerized, and games' key moments are决дently influenced by statistical data and a team's current situation. A notable game-ending incident in the 2018 World Cup between Croatia and Russia highlighted the importance of maintaining possession and avoiding errors in critical scenarios. Our project involves creating a sophisticated reward system for policy-learning algorithms that can accurately assess various in-game situations, taking into account factors like possession, location, game time, and even subtle actions like fouls or throwing the ball out of bounds. By simulating thousands of similar scenarios to predict the best course of action in situations where direct shot-on-goal probabilities are difficult to estimate, our system has demonstrated its value compared to traditional methods. A recent study on the impact of different approaches revealed that our customized system can significantly benefit a team's performance in high-stakes situations, making it an essential tool for strategic decision-making in football games.

This study investigates the stability of solitary wave solutions in a specific anharmonic oscillator system under an external harmonic force. By incorporating an anharmonic oscillator into the harmonic Schrödinger harmonic oscillator system, we derive new inequalities essential for analyzing the system's properties. Although initial estimates of Gagliardo--Nirenberg and Poincaré types are not directly applicable to anharmonic oscillators, we develop comparable inequalities relevant to this context. Building on these revised inequalities, we prove the orbital stability of a non-linear solitary wave solution in a specific one-dimensional system under an anharmonic external force.
